_about: Shared petitions: the same ask, open in many places at once. County campaigns get one copy per county site, addressed to that county's own officials and counted toward its own goal; state campaigns get one copy per state; national ones a single copy. {county} and {state} are filled in. Posted by pipeline/campaigns.js (idempotent). 'hold' keeps a campaign from being posted until it's released.
started_by: Brayden Sanders, founder of County Commons

campaigns.title: Post every county payment online, every month, as searchable data
campaigns.why: Every check {county} writes is already a public record — but to see one, you have to file a request and wait. A monthly check register online (who was paid, how much, for what, from which fund) lets anyone follow the money without asking permission. Many counties and cities already do this. It costs little, because the county already keeps these records.

src.label: U.S. PIRG, Following the Money (state and local spending transparency)

campaigns.title: Disclose every award paid from county tax money that's handed to outside groups
campaigns.why: Some county tax money goes to outside organizations — economic development corporations, nonprofits, districts — and once it leaves, the county's bidding and public-records rules may not follow it. We ask {county} to post, for every dollar passed through: who received it, how much, what for, and what was promised in return. Public money should stay traceable all the way to the last receipt.

campaigns.title: Before buying or renewing license-plate cameras: a public hearing, the contract posted, and a yearly audit
campaigns.why: License-plate cameras record every car that passes, not just suspects, and the data can be shared with other agencies and companies. Before {county} buys or renews any, we ask for a public hearing, the contract and data-sharing rules posted online, a limit on how long the data is kept, and a yearly public report of how often it was searched and why. This isn't for or against cameras — it's about rules everyone can see.

src.label: This county's page on cameras and plate readers

campaigns.title: Publish the jail's numbers every month
campaigns.why: The county jail is one of the biggest costs in the budget. We ask {county} to post a short monthly report: how many people were held, how many were awaiting trial, the average stay, and how many were held for the state or federal government. Counties that track these numbers can see what's driving costs — and many already share them.

campaigns.title: Text people a reminder before their court date
campaigns.why: Many missed court dates are simple forgetting — and a missed date can mean a warrant, an arrest and days in jail. In New York City, text reminders and a clearer court notice cut missed court dates by 21–26% in a randomized study, at very low cost. We ask {county}'s courts and clerk to text reminders before every court date.

src.label: J-PAL summary of Fishbane, Ouss and Shah, Science (2020)

campaigns.title: Post meeting agendas a week ahead, and video or minutes of every meeting, online
campaigns.why: Decisions about {county}'s money are made in public meetings, but working people can't always be there. We ask that every agenda be posted online at least a week before the meeting, with its supporting documents, and that video or full minutes of every meeting be posted afterward. If you can't attend, you should still be able to see what was decided and why.

campaigns.title: Require every county, city and school district in {state} to post its payments online
campaigns.why: Instead of a separate fight in every county, one state law can require every local government in {state} to post its check register online each month — who was paid, how much, and for what. The records already exist; this makes them easy to see.

campaigns.title: Set statewide rules for license-plate camera data in {state}
campaigns.why: License-plate cameras are spreading fast, and the rules for their data differ town to town. We ask {state} lawmakers to set statewide limits: how long the data can be kept, who it can be shared with, a warrant or written reason to search it, and a yearly public report from every agency that uses it.

src.label: National Conference of State Legislatures, license-plate reader laws by state

campaigns.title: Make every {state} prison an accredited school for earning a living
campaigns.why: Nearly everyone in prison comes home. We ask {state} to make every prison an accredited place to learn — job training and education that end in a recognized credential, open to everyone held there. A RAND review of decades of studies found people who took part in prison education had 43% lower odds of returning to prison than those who didn't, and that it can save money by keeping people from coming back.

src.label: RAND, Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (2013)

campaigns.title: Make every prison in America an accredited school for earning a living
campaigns.why: Nearly everyone in prison comes home. We ask Congress to require and fund accredited job training and education in every federal prison, and to help states do the same — training that ends in a recognized credential. A RAND review of decades of studies found people who took part in prison education had 43% lower odds of returning to prison than those who didn't.

src.label: RAND, Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (2013)

campaigns.title: Keep calls from prison and jail affordable, and keep in-person visits
campaigns.why: Staying connected to family and friends is one of the best things for people inside and for the neighbors they come home to. A 2022 law passed with support from both parties let the FCC cap the price of prison and jail calls; the caps set in 2024 were raised in October 2025. We ask Congress and the FCC to keep calls affordable — and to keep in-person visits from being replaced by paid video.

campaigns.title: Require project-by-project reporting of federal money sent to local governments
campaigns.why: Counties received $48.5 billion in federal pandemic relief. More than half was reported only as "revenue replacement," so the public can't trace it to what it bought. We ask Congress to require that federal money sent to local governments be reported project by project — what it paid for, who was paid, and what it delivered.

src.label: U.S. Treasury, State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds reporting

campaigns.title: Open unused county land to community gardens on a $1 revocable license
campaigns.why: Newark, New Jersey leases vacant lots to residents for $1 a year through its Adopt-a-Lot program, and Baltimore grants free, revocable licenses — neither sells the land. Brown County, Wisconsin has run community gardens through its Extension office since 1996: 13 gardens and 386 plots. We ask {county} to let residents garden unused county land under a simple revocable license.

src.label: UW–Madison Extension, Brown County community gardens

campaigns.title: Create a county food policy council with seats for growers, schools and the food bank
campaigns.why: A food policy council brings local government, growers, schools and food banks to one table. 283 were active in the U.S. as of 2020, according to a CDC journal study, and many are created by a local government resolution. We ask {county} to create one by resolution.

src.label: Preventing Chronic Disease (CDC), food policy councils
Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future

campaigns.title: Start a community seed library in the county library system
campaigns.why: Open-pollinated seed can be saved and replanted; hybrid seed does not come true from saved seed, and patented seed can’t legally be saved. A seed library lends seed at planting time and takes back a share at harvest. Seed Savers Exchange keeps a collection of more than 25,000 varieties. We ask {county} and its library to start one.

src.label: University of Maryland Extension, saving seeds

campaigns.title: Set a goal for buying local food in county institutions, and ask school districts to do the same
campaigns.why: U.S. schools bought $789 million of local food in the 2013–14 school year, up 105% in two years, according to USDA. Districts with farm-to-school programs spent about 20% of their food budgets on local food (USDA 2019 Farm to School Census). We ask {county} to set a local-food buying goal for the jail and other county institutions, and to ask school districts to do the same.

campaigns.title: Support a local food hub with shared cold storage and a commercial kitchen
campaigns.why: Food hubs collect produce from local farms and sell it to schools, hospitals and stores. In Michigan State University’s 2025 national survey, more than half of food hubs said grants made their sales to institutions possible. We ask {county} to support a food hub with shared cold storage and a commercial kitchen that local growers and food businesses can rent.

campaigns.title: Support a local nonprofit’s application for a USDA Community Food Projects grant
campaigns.why: USDA’s Community Food Projects program funds local food projects up to $400,000, with a one-to-one match. Nonprofits apply, not counties — but county land, Extension staff time or a site can count toward the match. We ask {county} to offer a letter of support and an in-kind match to a local nonprofit that applies.

campaigns.title: Start an optional jail garden with the county Extension office
campaigns.why: In Smith County, Texas, people in the jail grow a garden and give all of the produce to the East Texas Food Bank — more than 160,000 pounds by the food bank CEO’s estimate. Garland County, Arkansas’s detention center works with the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture and donates produce to a food bank. We ask {county} to start an optional jail garden with its Extension office.

campaigns.title: Include classroom, shop, kitchen and garden space in any new or renovated county jail
campaigns.why: A RAND review of decades of studies found that people who took part in education while locked up had 43% lower odds of returning to prison. In 2023, about 70% of people in U.S. jails had not been convicted of the charge they were held on (Bureau of Justice Statistics). We ask {county} to include classroom, trade-shop, kitchen and garden space in any new or renovated jail.

campaigns.title: Pilot an optional, paid jail crew that builds homes with a licensed builder and a nonprofit
campaigns.why: Garland County, Arkansas’s jail runs a farm program, and Garland County Habitat for Humanity has built more than 170 homes since 1995. A federally funded review of studies found that vocational training in prison raised employment after release more than other education did. We ask {county} to pilot an optional, paid crew that builds homes alongside a licensed builder and a housing nonprofit.

src.label: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (meta-analysis)

campaigns.title: Fund a voluntary live-in program with housing, work and recovery that anyone may leave
campaigns.why: Bexar County, Texas runs a diversion center where people can choose treatment instead of jail. Job Corps is a federal live-in job-training program, rated in the Justice Department’s CrimeSolutions clearinghouse. We ask {county} to fund a voluntary live-in program with housing, paid work and recovery services that anyone may join or leave.

src.label: San Antonio Report, Bexar County diversion center

campaigns.title: Receive resident petitions at a public meeting and post a written answer
campaigns.why: Stanford researchers found people who took part in deliberative polls followed politics more closely and voted more, nearly a year later. We ask {county}’s governing body to set a standing agenda time to receive petitions residents deliver, and to post a written answer to each one.

campaigns.title: Hold a public hearing on how the general fund is divided before the budget is adopted
campaigns.why: Some county money is set aside by law for one purpose — roads, 911, libraries. The general fund is the part the county’s governing body divides each year. We ask {county} to hold a public hearing on how the general fund is divided before it adopts the budget.

campaigns.title: Direct {state} Medicaid to cover produce prescriptions
campaigns.why: Several states have federal approval to use Medicaid for nutrition support, according to KFF. A peer-reviewed study of 9 produce-prescription programs at 22 sites, with 3,881 participants, found people ate about one more serving of fruits and vegetables a day and had lower blood pressure, body weight and blood sugar, and less food insecurity. We ask {state} lawmakers and the governor to have the state Medicaid program cover produce prescriptions.

campaigns.title: Require {state} agencies to publish purchase-card spending item by item
campaigns.why: Oklahoma posts its state purchase-card transactions online, searchable by merchant and item and updated monthly. Ohio’s OhioCheckbook put state transactions online. A U.S. Government Accountability Office review found 41–48% of sampled federal purchase-card transactions failed basic controls. We ask {state} lawmakers to require state agencies to publish purchase-card spending item by item.

campaigns.title: Require federal agencies to publish government purchase-card spending item by item
campaigns.why: Federal purchase cards carried $39.4 billion across about 82 million transactions in fiscal 2025, according to the General Services Administration, and the card networks record each purchase’s merchant, category and amount. GSA publishes totals. We ask Congress to require agencies to publish the transactions themselves.
